identity.title: Passive leg raise: hemodynamic response (BP/pulse pressure or POCUS VTI rise >=10-12%) within 60-90 s of raising legs 45 deg from semi-recumbent

technique.how: Start semi-recumbent (trunk 45 deg). Record baseline cardiac output surrogate (LVOT VTI, pulse-contour CO, bioreactance) or, less reliably, arterial pulse pressure. Using the bed controls, lower the trunk flat and raise the legs to 45 deg without touching the patient; re-measure within 60-90 s. Positive = CO/VTI rise >=10%. Return to baseline and confirm reversibility.
technique.prerequisites: A real-time flow measurement (echo VTI, pulse contour, bioreactance) gives the validated result; pulse pressure alone is a weak substitute. Use the bed, not manual lifting, to avoid pain/sympathetic stimulation.
technique.contraindications: Raised intracranial pressure, unstable pelvic/leg fractures, intra-abdominal hypertension, compression stockings/venous obstruction, and inability to lie flat.

interpretation.positive_finding: A CO/VTI rise >=10% predicts that a fluid bolus will raise cardiac output (pooled sensitivity 85%, specificity 91%, AUC 0.95), supporting a fluid trial in shock or oliguria. A pulse-pressure rise is specific (83%) but insensitive (56-58%).
interpretation.negative_finding: No CO rise makes fluid responsiveness unlikely (LR- about 0.16 with flow measurement) and argues for vasopressors/inotropes or diuresis rather than more fluid. A negative pulse-pressure PLR is unreliable for excluding fluid responsiveness.
interpretation.pitfalls: BP or pulse-pressure based PLR misses about half of responders. Fluid responsiveness is not the same as needing fluid: a positive test in a patient without hypoperfusion is not a reason to give volume.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive PLR (CO-based): give a fluid challenge; negative: stop fluids and consider vasoactive support. PP-based positive is usable, PP-based negative is not.

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness (CO rise after volume expansion), PLR assessed by cardiac output change (threshold ~10%)
estimates.population: Adults with acute circulatory failure; 21 studies, 991 patients, 995 fluid challenges
estimates.reference_standard: Increase in cardiac output after a fluid challenge (study-specific threshold, usually >=15%)
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.85/(1-0.91) = 9.4; LR- = (1-0.85)/0.91 = 0.16, from pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.91
estimates.quote: For the PLR-induced changes in CO, the pooled sensitivity was 0.85 (0.81-0.88) and the pooled specificity was 0.91 (0.88-0.93)

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness, PLR assessed by arterial pulse pressure change
estimates.population: Adults with acute circulatory failure; 8 studies, 432 fluid challenges
estimates.reference_standard: Increase in cardiac output after a fluid challenge
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.56/(1-0.83) = 3.3; LR- = (1-0.56)/0.83 = 0.53, from pooled sensitivity 0.56 and specificity 0.83
estimates.quote: the pooled sensitivity was 0.56 (0.49-0.53), the pooled specificity was 0.83 (0.77-0.88) and the pooled area under the ROC curve was 0.77

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness, PLR assessed by flow variables (cardiac output or derivatives)
estimates.population: Adults (ICU/OR/ED studies); 23 studies, 1,013 patients, 1,034 fluid challenges
estimates.reference_standard: Fluid challenge response (gold standard as defined per study)
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.85/(1-0.92) = 10.6; LR- = (1-0.85)/0.92 = 0.16, from reported sensitivity 85% and specificity 92% for flow variables
estimates.quote: vs sensitivity of 85% [95% CI, 78-90] and specificity of 92% [95% CI, 87-94], respectively; p < 0.001

estimates.target_condition: Fluid responsiveness, PLR assessed by pulse pressure change
estimates.population: Adults (ICU/OR/ED studies); subset of 23 studies using pulse pressure
estimates.reference_standard: Fluid challenge response (gold standard as defined per study)
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.58/(1-0.83) = 3.4; LR- = (1-0.58)/0.83 = 0.51, from reported sensitivity 58% and specificity 83%
estimates.quote: sensitivity of 58% [95% CI, 44-70] and specificity of 83% [95% CI, 68-92] vs sensitivity of 85%

sources.citation: Monnet X, Marik P, Teboul JL. Passive leg raising for predicting fluid responsiveness: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Intensive Care Med. 2016;42(12):1935-1947.
Cherpanath TG, Hirsch A, Geerts BF, et al. Predicting Fluid Responsiveness by Passive Leg Raising: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of 23 Clinical Trials. Crit Care Med. 2016;44(5):981-991.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Raised intracranial pressure, unstable fractures, intra-abdominal hypertension, venous compression devices, or when no flow measurement is available and the question is ruling OUT fluid responsiveness.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A negative flow-based PLR in a hypotensive patient means more fluid is unlikely to help; escalate to vasopressor/inotrope decisions and look for obstructive or cardiogenic causes.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Reproducibility depends on the CO measurement (echo VTI is operator dependent); the manoeuvre itself must be done with the bed, semi-recumbent to legs-up, with measurement within 60-90 s.
safety_scope.skill_assumption: For the VTI variant, operator must obtain a reproducible apical 5-chamber LVOT VTI before and within 90 s after the manoeuvre; the BP/PP variant requires no imaging skill but is insensitive.

extraction_notes: Both meta-analyses are quantified from abstracts (full text not in PMC). Monnet 2016: the abstract prints the pulse-pressure sensitivity CI as '0.49-0.53', which cannot bracket 0.56 and is presumably a typographical error, so the CI is left null and the point estimate retained. Threshold quote for CO-based PLR: 'best threshold was a PLR-induced increase in CO >=10 +/- 2 %' (Monnet abstract). All LRs computed from pooled sens/spec. Estimates are separated by measurement method (flow vs pulse pressure), which is the dominant driver of performance; setting is ICU/mixed critically ill adults, not ward patients.
